# Book I, Proposition 8

*Side, side, side*

> If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/08.svg" alt="The figure for Proposition I.8" width="360"></p>

## Euclid's proof

Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the base EF;

I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on the point E and the straight line BC on EF,

the point C will also coincide with F,

because BC is equal to EF.

Then, BC coinciding with EF,

BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;

for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,

then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.

But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]

Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA, AC should not coincide with ED, DF;

they will therefore coincide,

so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.

If therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop08.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop08.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- The triangle `ABC`, read starting from `B`, is still a triangle: three points
that are not on one straight line, in whatever order we name them. -/
theorem Prop8.triangle {A B C : Point} (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle B C A := by
  rintro ⟨L, hB, hC, hA⟩
  exact h ⟨L, hA, hB, hC⟩

/-- What Euclid sees when he lays BC along EF: a point `P` on the straight line
`EF`, on the same side of `E` as `F`, and as far from `E` as `F` is, is `F`
itself. -/
theorem Prop8.coincide {E F P : Point} {L : Line} (hE : OnLine E L) (hF : OnLine F L)
    (hP : OnLine P L) (hEF : E ≠ F) (hray : ¬ Between P E F) (h : ‖E P‖ = ‖E F‖) :
    P = F := by
  by_cases hPF : P = F
  · exact hPF
  have hEP : E ≠ P := ne_of_len_eq h hEF
  /- Of the three points E, P, F on one straight line, one lies between the other
     two. P can't be on the far side of E from F; and if P were short of F, or
     beyond it, then EF would be equal to EF together with something. -/
  rcases between_cases hEP hPF hEF hE hP hF with hEPF | hPEF | hEFP
  · have hsum : ‖E P‖ + ‖P F‖ = ‖E F‖ := len_add_of_between hEPF
    rw [h] at hsum
    have hlt : ‖E F‖ < ‖E F‖ + ‖P F‖ := CommonNotion5 (len_pos hPF)
    rw [hsum] at hlt
    exact absurd hlt (lt_irrefl _)
  · exact absurd hPEF hray
  · have hsum : ‖E F‖ + ‖F P‖ = ‖E P‖ := len_add_of_between hEFP
    rw [h] at hsum
    have hlt : ‖E F‖ < ‖E F‖ + ‖F P‖ := CommonNotion5 (len_pos (Ne.symm hPF))
    rw [hsum] at hlt
    exact absurd hlt (lt_irrefl _)

/-- Two points on the same side of the straight line through `E` and `F` are on
the same side of `EF`, whichever way we name that line: two points fix one
straight line. -/
theorem Prop8.sameSide {G D E F : Point} {L : Line} (hEF : E ≠ F) (hE : OnLine E L)
    (hF : OnLine F L) (h : SameSide G D L) : SameSideOf G D E F := by
  refine ⟨hEF, fun M hEM hFM => ?_⟩
  rw [← line_unique hEF hE hF hEM hFM]
  exact h

/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base
equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal
straight lines. -/
theorem Prop8 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the
  -- base EF;
  -- I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on
  -- the point E and the straight line BC on EF,
  /- To lay BC along EF we need the straight line EF itself (Postulate 1). The
     rule of superposition then sets B on E, sends C along the ray from E through
     F, and lets us choose the side of EF on which A comes down: D's side, so
     that the two triangles lie over one another, as Euclid's word "applied"
     means. The copy of ABC is `G E C'`: C lands at `C'` and A at `G`. -/
  have hEF : E ≠ F := hDEF.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩ := Postulate1 E F hEF
  have hD_EF : ¬ OnLine D EF := fun hD => hDEF ⟨EF, hD, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩
  obtain ⟨C', G, hC'_EF, hC'_ray, hGD_EF, hEC', hC'G, hGE, -, hEGC', -⟩ :=
    superposition (Prop8.triangle hABC) hE_EF hF_EF hEF hD_EF
  -- the point C will also coincide with F,
  -- because BC is equal to EF.
  have hC'F : C' = F := Prop8.coincide hE_EF hF_EF hC'_EF hEF hC'_ray (hEC'.trans hBC)
  -- Then, BC coinciding with EF,
  -- BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;
  /- The sides BA, AC have been carried to GE, GF, and they are equal to ED, DF. -/
  have hGE_DE : ‖G E‖ = ‖D E‖ := hGE.trans hAB
  have hGF_DF : ‖G F‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    calc ‖G F‖ = ‖F G‖ := len_symm G F
      _ = ‖C' G‖ := by rw [hC'F]
      _ = ‖C A‖ := hC'G
      _ = ‖A C‖ := len_symm C A
      _ = ‖D F‖ := hAC
  -- for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with
  -- ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,
  -- then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and
  -- meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its
  -- extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another
  -- point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same
  -- extremity with it.
  /- G and D are on the same side of EF: superposition put G there. -/
  have hGD_side : SameSideOf G D E F := Prop8.sameSide hEF hE_EF hF_EF hGD_EF
  -- But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]
  -- Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA,
  -- AC should not coincide with ED, DF;
  -- they will therefore coincide,
  /- Our I.7 is stated positively: two such points are one and the same point.
     So Euclid's reduction to the impossible is a single step here. -/
  have hGD : G = D := Prop7 hGD_side hGE_DE hGF_DF
  -- so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.
  /- The angle BAC was carried to the angle EGC', and G is D, C' is F. -/
  have hEGC'_EDF : ∠ E G C' = ∠ E D F := CommonNotion4.angle rfl hGD hC'F
  exact hEGC'.symm.trans hEGC'_EDF
  -- If therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**Picking up a triangle.** As in I.4, Euclid lifts the triangle ABC and lays it on DEF, something none of his postulates allows. Here that is one named rule, [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean), in the form LeanEuclid gives it, which folds System E's two superposition rules into one. Nothing actually moves: the rule hands us a fresh copy of ABC, with B on E, C somewhere on the ray from E through F, and A on whichever side of EF we ask for, every side and angle kept. Avigad, Dean and Mumma allow superposition only for proving facts about a figure already drawn, never for building new ones, and to respect that, the certificate's checks let only I.4 and I.8 cite it.

**"The point C will also coincide with F."** Euclid's reason, "because BC is equal to EF", is only half of it. The other half is the ray: C lands on F's side of E, not beyond E the other way, and that is what "the straight line BC on EF" is there to secure. `Prop8.coincide` says it out loud. On the straight line EF, on F's side of E, the one point as far from E as F is, is F. Any other would make EF equal to EF together with something, and the whole is greater than the part.

**Which side A comes down on.** Euclid never says that A lands on the same side of EF as D, but I.7 needs exactly that. On opposite sides, two points can be at the same distances from E and F without being the same point: think of D and its mirror image in EF. So we ask the superposition rule for D's side, which is what "applied to the triangle DEF" means. `Prop8.sameSide` then checks that "the same side of EF" doesn't depend on which straight line through E and F we name, since two points fix one straight line (System E, Generalities 1). As in I.3, Lean needs that straight line before it can lay anything along it, so Postulate 1 is on the certificate although Euclid doesn't cite it.

**Falling beside.** Euclid supposes BA, AC "do not coincide with ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF". Heath notes that the Greek word means "to pass by without touching," "to miss" or "to deviate" (vol. 1, p. 262). Our I.7 is stated positively, so that two such points are one and the same point, and Euclid's reduction to the impossible becomes a single citation of `Prop7`: G is D.

**Why only the angle.** Heath: "It is to be observed that in I. 8 Euclid is satisfied with proving the equality of the vertical angles and does not, as in I. 4, add that the triangles are equal, and the remaining angles are equal respectively. The reason is no doubt (as pointed out by Proclus and by Savile after him) that, when once the vertical angles are proved equal, the rest follows from I. 4, and there is no object in proving again what has been proved already" (vol. 1, p. 262).

**Other roads.** Proclus preserves a proof by Philo that lays ABC on the far side of EF and uses I.5 in place of I.7. Heath: "This alternative proof avoids the use of I. 7, and it is elegant; but it is inconvenient in one respect, since three cases have to be distinguished" (vol. 1, p. 263). He prizes I.7 for its own sake, quoting Charles Dodgson: "of all plane figures that can be made by hingeing rods together, the three-sided ones (and these only) are rigid" (vol. 1, p. 261). Hilbert, who made side–angle–side an axiom, proves side–side–side from it as a theorem, with no moving of figures at all, and Beeson, Narboux and Wiedijk, checking Book I from Tarski's axioms, had no superposition to call on either. And Heath finds the theorem in Aristotle, who, "speaking of the rainbow", observes "that, if equal rays be reflected from one and the same point to one and the same point, the points at which reflection takes place are on the circumference of a circle" (vol. 1, p. 262).

**The modern way.** With vectors, |B − C|² = |A − B|² + |A − C|² − 2 (B − A)·(C − A), so the three sides fix the dot product, and with it the angle at A: this is the law of cosines, cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / 2bc. Superposition has a modern name too: a rigid motion of the plane, and any two triangles with the same three sides are carried one onto the other, corner to corner, by exactly one of them.
